24.0.s.en: (1) David's order to number the people

24.0.0.en: The text states here that it was the Lord who moved David to number the people, whereas in the First Book of Chronicles (1 Chr 21:1) this is attributed to Satan. The explanation of this is that the Lord does not drive people to evil. When people incline of themselves toward the enticement of the enemy of good, He leaves them to do what they wish, and this takes place with God's permission.

24.0.1.en: The purpose of David's desire for the numbering was to boast of their multitude, and the people supported him in that. This purpose was not in harmony with the will of God, who had prescribed the taking of a census for specific religious and ritual purposes that God had already appointed for them (Ex 30:11): paying a ransom for the males, or counting those fit for military service, or preparing the Levites who would take part in the service of the house of the Lord...

24.0.2.en: So the kindling of God's anger was because of the sin of David and the people, which was fundamentally pride. He permitted David to order the numbering, but He was angry about it, and so He punished him, as we shall see in this chapter. God's anger had been kindled many times before against the people because of their sins, from the days of Moses and before, until now. He permitted them to be humbled in Egypt and the murmurers to fall dead in the wilderness of Sinai, and He was also angry with the people because of Saul's sin in the matter of the Gibeonites (ch. 21). Therefore it says, "And again the anger of the Lord was kindled."... David's sin in the numbering was great, for the following reasons:

24.0.3.en: 1- Pride, as we mentioned, especially since he had been victorious in many wars and his kingdom had grown wide, so he wanted to know his strength and boast in it. The people shared with him in the pride, and they forgot that God alone was the cause of their victories.

24.0.4.en: 2- He did not consult God before the numbering.

24.0.5.en: 3- Perhaps after the numbering he wanted to use his strength in new wars or in some works of his own that God had not commanded.

24.0.6.en: 4- It is mentioned that he ordered the numbering of Israel and Judah, separating the tribe of Judah from the rest of the tribes, because David was of this tribe, and the number of this tribe had increased, so he wanted to boast of it.

24.0.7.en: 5- Perhaps he had other personal purposes, such as using the people to carry out some of his interests or to collect taxes from them.

24.0.8.en: 6- He did not collect from them the value of the ransom, which is half a shekel, offered to the Temple as the Law prescribed (Ex 30:12).

24.0.9.en: 7- The Book of Chronicles (1 Chr 27:23, 24) tells us that he counted those who were under twenty years of age, and this is contrary to the Law.

24.0.10.en: 8- He forgot that the people are the people of God and not his own people, for God alone is the One who blesses them and boasts of them because they are His workmanship, so it is not right to steal the glory of God.

24.1.0.en: The king commanded Joab, the commander of his army, to go through the regions of the land from the farthest north (Dan) to the farthest south (Beersheba) to number the people and bring him the result.

24.2.0.en: Joab wanted to dissuade David from his desire to number the people, praying that the Lord would multiply His people a hundredfold so that the king might look upon their multitude with joy, and he asked him what he desired by this request. This was a wise act on Joab's part, for although he was violent and bloody, he warned the king of the danger of numbering the people, since this carries pride, but he warned him with great courtesy, for Joab was careful for the good of the king and the kingdom.

24.3.0.en: David did not listen to the attempt of Joab and the captains of the army to dissuade him from his desire, but rebuked them and insisted strongly on carrying out his command. So they were compelled to yield to his wish, and they went out from him to go through the regions of the kingdom and number the people.

24.3.1.en: It is not wise to neglect the advice of others. Rather, let us accustom ourselves to benefit from the counsel of the wise around us and not insist on our own opinions in pride, even if the guidance comes from people younger than we are, or lower in position or knowledge.

24.4.0.en: These verses describe the route of the journey made by Joab and the captains of the army.

24.4.1.en: They began by crossing the Jordan River to the east bank and passed near "Aroer," one of the cities of the tribe of Gad. Their passing was to the right of the city, in the direction of the town of "Jazer," and they came to Gilead to number the tribes dwelling there, the two tribes of Reuben and Gad. Then they continued to "Tahtim-hodshi" in the land of "Tahtim," and from there they reached "Dan-jaan," then turned around to Zidon, then to the stronghold of Tyre and to all the cities that the children of Israel had taken from the Hivites and the Canaanites. On the way back toward the south they gathered the numbers of the tribes dwelling west of the Jordan until they reached the lands of Judah and then Beersheba in the far south. Their journey thus covered all the lands in which the children of Israel dwell, east and west of the Jordan. It took nine months and twenty days, and ended with their arrival at Jerusalem, the same city from which they had set out to begin their work. The route mentioned is a circuit from the south to the east of the Jordan, and from there to the farthest north of Palestine, then to the west, returning to the west of the Jordan River, and then from its farthest north to its farthest south.

24.5.0.en: On the return of Joab and his men, they presented the king with a report of the results of the census. It showed that the number of males of the tribes of Israel (apart from the tribe of Judah) from twenty years old and upward was 800 thousand. This number does not include the Levites or the tribe of Benjamin, which lay at the end of the return route, so it appears that the men who carried out the census had become exhausted, in addition to not having been convinced from the start of the usefulness of this numbering. The number of males of twenty years and upward of the tribe of Judah was 500 thousand, so the total of the tribes of Israel with the tribe of Judah added to them is 1,300,000 (one million three hundred thousand). If the number of soldiers represents about a fifth or a sixth of the people, this means that the number of the people at that time reached 6 or 7 million. This is a great number, owing to God's blessing and care for them.

24.5.1.en: The First Book of Chronicles (1 Chr 21:5) states that the number of Israel was 1,100,000, which is 300 thousand more than their number here, and it also states that the number of Judah was 470 thousand men, which is 30 thousand fewer than their number here. The explanation of this difference is as follows:

24.5.2.en: The extra three hundred thousand in Chronicles are those actually enlisted permanently to bear arms, whereas the eight hundred thousand are those fit to bear arms if necessity calls. There is another opinion about the three hundred thousand, namely the difference between the number of the enlisted of the tribes of Israel mentioned in Chronicles, that is 1,100,000, and their number here, which is 800,000. This opinion says that the Book of Samuel mentions that the eight hundred thousand are "men of valor," that is, tested men of greater ability in war, while the remaining three hundred thousand are of lesser ability.

24.5.3.en: Likewise the 30 thousand whom the Book of Chronicles did not include in the numbering are "the chosen men of Israel" (ch. 6:1), who were charged with keeping security and with the royal guard permanently.

24.5.4.en: It is noted that the tribe of Levi was not counted here because they do not take part in wars but are consecrated to the service of the Lord. As for the tribe of Benjamin, their number may be the thirty thousand, which is the difference between the number of the tribe of Judah here and what corresponds to it in the Book of Chronicles.

24.6.0.en: David felt his fault and regretted the command he had issued to carry out the numbering, and he confessed to the Lord that what he had done was folly without justification, and he began to beseech the Lord to forgive him this fault. This shows an important trait in David, namely repentance, by which he obtains God's favor and mercy whatever his sins may be. It also shows that the numbering was not from God, because David did not rejoice but was grieved, and his heart smote him.

24.6.1.en: We often rush after our personal desires and make decisions that we later regret. Let us be patient in our choices so that we do not fall into error and then regret and grieve.

24.7.0.en: David spent the night weeping, regretting his fault, praying to the Lord to pardon him and forgive him, and in the morning of the next day Gad the prophet came to him with a message from the Lord.

24.8.0.en: The message of the Lord that Gad the prophet carried to David was to give him a choice among three punishments, one of which the Lord must bring upon him. This shows God's justice in punishing sin, and at the same time His mercy in giving David a choice of one of the punishments.

24.9.0.en: Gad conveyed to David the text of the message, and the three punishments among which he gave David the choice were: the first: that there be a famine in the land lasting seven years.

24.9.1.en: The second: that his enemies pursue him for three months while he flees before them.

24.9.2.en: The third: that the Lord strike the people with a pestilence for three days.

24.9.3.en: It is stated in the Book of Chronicles (1 Chr 21:12) that the famine in the first punishment was for three years and not seven years as it appears here. The explanation of this difference is that the Book of Chronicles did not include the period that precedes the beginning of the famine and follows its end, which is usually lighter in severity than the middle period, in which the intensity of the famine is at its height.

24.10.0.en: David was perplexed and felt that he had put himself in a predicament from which there was no escape. After thinking, he chose one of the three things in which he would be under the Lord's vast mercy, and not fall into the choice that would put him at the mercy of his enemies. For the Lord wounds and binds up, crushes and His hands heal, disciplines and then has compassion, whereas man is hard of heart and strikes without mercy.

24.11.0.en: To the appointed time: most likely the time of offering the evening sacrifice, which is offered every day in the house of the Lord. David's choice was to be in the hand of God, that is, the first punishment or the third, which is "the pestilence." So the Lord carried out the third punishment and destroyed by the pestilence 70 thousand from all the tribes, from the farthest north to the farthest south. They kept falling throughout the day, from the morning until the time of the daily evening offering (1 Kgs 18:29). The punishment that came upon them treats the problem of the pride of David and the people in the greatness of their number, for behold, their number is diminished so that they might not be proud but rely on God alone.

24.12.0.en: Threshingfloor: that is, a threshing place, a place for gathering and storing the produce of the land.

24.12.1.en: Araunah the Jebusite: the name "Araunah" appears in Samuel and "Ornan" in Chronicles, and the two names are for one person who owned a threshingfloor on Mount Moriah, east of Jerusalem. David bought it from him to offer burnt offerings on it, and it is the same mountain on which Solomon's Temple was built (1 Chr 21). One of the angels, the one charged with carrying out the punishment, continued in it until the turn came to Jerusalem to destroy its inhabitants. But the Lord had compassion on "the city of the great King" and accepted the supplications of its people and their repentance, and He commanded the angel to stop the plague, saying it was enough for those who had died up to that time, who, as in the preceding verse, were 70 thousand.

24.12.2.en: When the command was given to the angel to stop the plague, he was at that time at a granary owned by a man of Jebusite origin who had embraced Judaism. This confirms God's mercy and compassion on David and his repentant people who cried out to Him, so He stopped the plague.

24.13.s.en: (3) The building of the altar and the lifting of the plague

24.13.0.en: David saw the angel charged with carrying out the plague, and he grieved greatly and suffered, confessing his fault once again, and he acknowledged that his people had not sinned: if he deserved the punishment, these had not shared his fault. As a faithful shepherd who has compassion on his flock, he asked the Lord not to destroy his people but to destroy him and his father's house in place of the innocent people. This shows how much David took responsibility for his fault, although the people truly shared with him the feeling of pride in the greatness of their number and the boasting of their strength. But he wanted to redeem his people by bearing the punishment himself and his household in place of the people, after the likeness of Christ the Redeemer. Yet God punished all, because all had sinned.

24.14.0.en: The Lord answered the prayers of David and the entreaties of his people, and He had mercy on them and sent Gad to David to tell him to go up to Mount Moriah and build there an altar to the Lord on the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite, and to offer sacrifices to the Lord as an atonement for himself and for the people. The Book of Chronicles (1 Chr 21:20) states that God opened the eyes of Araunah the Jebusite and he saw the angel of the Lord, and so he sensed the seriousness of the matter and the coming of King David to him.

24.14.1.en: The Lord does not rejoice in punishing His children, but feels their afflictions and grieves for what befalls them, as Isaiah the prophet says: "In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them" (Isa 63:9). Let us always turn to God, asking for His many mercies and His countless kindnesses.

24.15.0.en: David carried out the command of the Lord that had come to him by the mouth of Gad the prophet, and came to the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite. Araunah saw the king and his men coming toward him, so he went out to meet him and bowed down before him as an expression of his respect for him.

24.16.0.en: Araunah asked David the reason for his coming to him, and David told him that it was for the purpose of buying his threshingfloor in order to build on it an altar to the Lord on which to offer sacrifices, so that the plague would be stayed from the people.

24.17.0.en: Araunah was a generous man who showed his readiness to give up ownership of the threshingfloor to the king so that he might offer on it whatever sacrifices he wished. He even wanted to donate the sacrifices and the wooden threshing instruments used in threshing, for David to use as fuel on the altar. All this Araunah placed at the king's disposal without payment. Araunah prayed for the king that the Lord would accept from him the offerings he presented to Him, and would answer his prayer and lift the plague from the people. Because of Araunah's love, which appeared in his welcoming the king to build the altar on his land and his readiness to give his animals and the threshing instruments to help in offering the sacrifice, God gave him the grace not only that the plague be stayed at his threshingfloor but also that the altar be built on his land, and perhaps he also saw the destroying angel as he stopped the plague. For God blesses everyone whose heart is full of love and giving.

24.18.1.en: David refused to accept this free offer from Araunah, because he did not wish to offer burnt offerings that were not from his own possessions and at the expense of another, but wanted the honoring of the Lord to be from his own money. In keeping with the king's determination, Araunah agreed to sell the threshingfloor and the oxen and their implements to the king for 50 shekels of silver, which he received from the king (750 grams of silver), and this was the suitable price at that time.

24.19.0.en: David built the altar and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings to the Lord, and the Lord accepted those offerings in answer to David's prayers for his people. The Book of Chronicles (1 Chr 21:26) states that fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offerings as a sign of their acceptance by the Lord. The plague was stayed from the people, and from that day David began to offer his sacrifices and the sacrifices of his people in that place.

24.19.1.en: Mount Moriah, on which David offered his sacrifice in the field of Araunah the Jebusite, is the same place where Abraham long before offered his son Isaac as a sacrifice (Gen 22), and there is a Jewish tradition that it is the same place where the Lord of glory Jesus Christ was crucified. The three events all revolve around the idea of redemption, which was accomplished on the Cross.

24.19.2.en: Thank God who loved you and redeemed you on the Cross, and whose mercies are open to you to forgive all your sins when you come to Him repentant. So hold fast to confession and Holy Communion that you may enjoy God's work in you, and do not despair however many your sins may be.

24.19.3.en: The life of David - the youngest, the eighth son of Jesse, and the meaning of his name is beloved (1 Sam 16:10, 11, 17:13-14). He lived in Bethlehem and tended his father's sheep, and he was fair in appearance and very courageous (1 Sam 17:

24.19.4.en: 34-36.) - Samuel anointed him king, and that was in the year 1065 B.C. (1 Sam 16). - Saul summoned him to play the harp for him so that the unclean spirit that had come upon him would depart from him (1 Sam 16:19-23). - He killed Goliath, and the women cheered for him more than for Saul, so the latter was enraged (1 Sam 17, 18). - He killed two hundred Philistines as a dowry for Michal the daughter of Saul and then married her (1 Sam 18). - He became a friend of Jonathan the son of Saul, then Saul tried to kill him, especially after David's victory over the Philistines, and Jonathan interceded to prevent him (1 Sam 19). - Saul tried to kill him with the spear, then tried to seize him in his house, and Michal helped him escape (1 Sam 19:11-17). - He fled to Samuel at Ramah and Naioth (1 Sam 19:18), and Saul sent messengers to seize him, and they prophesied there, then Saul came himself and prophesied (1 Sam 19). - He made a covenant with Jonathan, who gave him a sign of Saul's hatred of him, and when David was sure that he was trying to kill him, he fled after kissing Jonathan (1 Sam 20). - He fled to Nob, the city of the priests, and ate of the bread of the priests and took the sword of Goliath (1 Sam 21:1-9). - He fled to Gath, a city of the Philistines, and feigned madness, so Achish king of Gath did not seize him (1 Sam 21:10-15). - 400 men joined him, then he went to Moab and left his father and mother there, but he returned to Judah by the guidance of Gad the prophet (1 Sam 22), and Abiathar the priest, who had escaped from the hand of Saul, the killer of the priests, took refuge with him (1 Sam 22:20-23). - He defeated the Philistines and saved Keilah, then left it for Ziph because of Saul's pursuit of him, and he had 600 men with him (1 Sam 23:1-14). - Jonathan renewed the covenant with him, and Saul tried to seize him in the wilderness of Ziph, but an attack by the Philistines made him abandon his pursuit (1 Sam 23:15-28). - He went to En-gedi, and Saul pursued him there, but Saul fell into his hand, and David cut off the skirt of his robe and rebuked him for pursuing him, so Saul was ashamed before him and departed (1 Sam 24). - He asked Nabal for help, and Nabal rebuked his messengers, whereupon David arose to kill him and all his men, but Abigail with her apology and gifts stopped David from the evil, then Nabal died and David married Abigail (1 Sam 25). - Saul continued to pursue him and fell a second time into David's hand, and he took his spear and the cruse of water and rebuked him, so Saul apologized and departed from him (1 Sam 26). - He took refuge with Achish king of Gath, he and his men, and settled in Ziklag and attacked the pagan peoples south of Judah, so Achish thought that he had attacked his own people and trusted him (1 Sam 27). - The Philistines prepared to fight the children of Israel, and the chiefs of the Philistines refused to let David go out with them (1 Sam 29), and they defeated the children of Israel and killed Saul and his sons (1 Sam 31). - David's grief and his lament for Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam 1). - David reigned in Hebron over the tribe of Judah, and Ish-bosheth the son of Saul reigned in Mahanaim over the rest of the tribes (2 Sam 2). - The wars continued between the tribe of Judah and the rest of the tribes and ended after seven years with David reigning over all the tribes, and Abner killed Ish-bosheth, and David recovered Michal (2 Sam 2, 3, 4, 5). - David defeated the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and took their stronghold, and also defeated the Philistines (2 Sam 5). - He moved the ark of the covenant of God to Jerusalem with great honor and tried to build a house for the Lord, but God postponed that so that it would be done by the hand of his son Solomon (2 Sam 6, 7). - His victories over the surrounding peoples followed one after another, namely the Philistines, the Moabites and the Arameans (2 Sam 8). - David's kindness to the descendants of Saul, namely Mephibosheth (2 Sam 9). - The continuing victories of David over the Arameans and the Ammonites (2 Sam 10). - He sinned with the wife of Uriah and then killed him, and Nathan the prophet rebuked him and he repented (2 Sam 11, 12). - Amnon sinned with Tamar his sister, and Absalom killed him and then fled (2 Sam 13). - The return of Absalom and his winning over the people, and David's flight from before him (2 Sam 14, 15). - The frustrating of the counsel of Ahithophel to Absalom, then David's victory, the killing of Absalom and his return to Jerusalem (2 Sam 16, 17, 18, 19). - The quelling of the rebellion of Sheba the son of Bichri against David (2 Sam 20). - David satisfies the Gibeonites, and his successive victories over the Philistines (2 Sam 21). - David's song of victory and the list of his heroes (2 Sam 22, 23). - David's sin of numbering the people, God's plague of pestilence and its stopping, and the offering of the sacrifice on the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite (2 Sam 24). - David's old age and Adonijah's attempt to make himself king, then David's making Solomon king, Solomon's killing of Adonijah, and the death of David (1 Kgs 1, 2). David as a type of Christ: David is a type of Christ in many matters in his life, among them:

24.19.5.en: 1- David, the meaning of whose name is the beloved, and Christ is the beloved of the Father (Eph 1:6).

24.19.6.en: 2- David was handsome, ruddy, with beautiful eyes, and Christ is fairer than the children of men.

24.19.7.en: 3- David was from Bethlehem, and Christ likewise was born in Bethlehem.

24.19.8.en: 4- David was anointed secretly, and at the same time Saul was reigning openly over the kingdom, just as Christ reigns secretly in the hearts of those who believe in Him, while the power of Satan, who dominates the world, and his evils appear.

24.19.9.en: 5- David is the anointed of the Lord, whom Samuel anointed, and Christ was anointed by the coming of the Holy Spirit upon Him in the Jordan River.

24.19.10.en: 6- David was the youngest, neglected son, and Christ was born in humility in a manger of oxen.

24.19.11.en: 7- David was the faithful shepherd who redeemed his sheep when he killed the lion and the bear, and Christ is the Good Shepherd who laid down His life for His sheep by His death on the Cross.

24.19.12.en: 8- David went to ask about his brothers in the war, and Christ became incarnate to visit His brothers, the children of men, and redeem them. And as David endured the reproaches of his brothers, Christ endured the opposition and reproaches of the Jews.

24.19.13.en: 9- David killed Goliath the giant who reproached the people of God, and Christ bound Satan, who wars against the children of God.

24.19.14.en: 10- The women cheered and sang for David after his victory over Goliath, and we praise Christ our Savior at all times.

24.19.15.en: 11- David lived hunted by Saul, with no place in which to settle, and Christ lived detached, having nowhere to lay His head.

24.19.16.en: 12- David became king at the age of 30 years, just as Christ began His ministry at thirty years of age.

24.19.17.en: 13- David united the tribe of Judah with the rest of the tribes to be one kingdom, just as Christ united the Jews with the Gentiles in one faith.

24.19.18.en: 14- The distressed and the persecuted gathered around David, and he made them an army, and sinners and the weary gathered around Christ, and He turned them into an army of believers who conquer Satan by His power.

24.19.19.en: 15- David did good to the Ziphites, but they betrayed him and tried to hand him over to Saul, and Christ did good to Judas Iscariot and to the Jews whom He healed and fed, but they betrayed Him and crucified Him.

24.19.20.en: 16- Ish-bosheth, together with the rest of the tribes, rose up against David, and so also the whole world rose up against Christ and crucified Him.

24.19.21.en: 17- Just as David reigned over the tribe of Judah and then over the rest of the tribes, so Christ reigned in Jerusalem and then Judea and Samaria and to the ends of the earth.

24.19.22.en: 18- The warriors who suffered with David during his pursuit by Saul were glorified with him when he reigned and became the heroes of his war. So whoever endures sufferings for the sake of Christ on earth is glorified in the Kingdom of Heaven.
